column4: It explicitly creates the an'am for people with warmth and benefits, grounding the source's claim that herd animals are called na'am because they bring good and benefit.
It stages the flock's evening return and morning release, the exact herd movement and beauty developed in the section.
The animals carry burdens to distant lands, making concrete the source's mounted animal whose legs carry and the owner's merciful provision for it.
The next ayah broadens the section's riding scene to horses, mules, and donkeys made for riding and adornment before 16:9 turns to the way.
It explicitly joins the animal passage to a straight way and a deviating way. The source's dictionary form hâdî, the leading animal, gives bodily force to guidance and to the contrary route.
It says God made the an'am and that people are their mālikūn, directly matching the source's Rabb/mālik relation to a herd.
The cattle are made compliant, ridden, and eaten. This is the Qur'anic counterpart to the source's tamed mount and its useful service.
Benefits and drinks come from the same tamed animals, completing the source's account of the herd as ni'mah-bearing provision.
People who do not use heart, eyes, and ears are likened to cattle and said to be more astray. It states the source's reversal: a human can be more lost than the herd animal.
It again calls heedless people like an'am, then more astray in way, making the strayness of the source's camel a judgment on human direction.
Every dābbah is held by its forelock while the speaker says, “my Rabb is on a straight path.” Ownership, the animal's leading point, and the route all meet in one ayah.
A person is bewildered on the earth after devils entice him, while companions call him toward guidance. It gives the source's isolated stray scene and a concrete counter-call to a leading guide.
Moses uses his staff to knock leaves down for his sheep. It stages a keeper feeding a flock, behind the source's herd, pasture, and guiding animal.
At Madyan, two women hold their flocks back at the water until the shepherds leave. The ayah gives a precise herd, keeper, waiting place, and watering boundary.
Moses waters the two women's animals; 28:23 supplies the flock, and this ayah's own act is the keeper's relief of its need at the watering place.
David and Solomon judge a field damaged at night by a people's sheep. A flock that has ranged into another's crop makes herd ownership and responsible tending legally visible.
The Lord inspires the bees where to make dwellings. It gives an animal collective a divinely directed habitation, relevant to the source's bee “malīk” and herd under a guide.
The bees are told to follow the ways of their Rabb made easy, then produce healing drink. The source's hâdî image becomes an animal following divinely eased routes that yield benefit.
The messenger names “Allah's she-camel” and her watering turn. Divine possession and a camel's allotted access to water directly answer the source's ownerless-versus-owned camel.
The she-camel is Allah's sign and is to be left to graze in Allah's earth. It joins divine ownership, an identifiable animal, and pasture.
The she-camel is again Allah's sign, to eat in God's earth without harm. Its named owner and lawful grazing form the opposite of the source's unowned camel in wasteland.
Sacrificial camels are made among God's signs; they stand in rows, are named over, then feed both owner and needy. It is a dense Qur'anic scene of marked, directed camel use.
The hady may not be cleared by shaving until it reaches its appointed place. The source's H-D-Y leading form meets its animal-offering sense: a herd animal has a directed destination.
The ayah protects sacrificial animals and their garlands. The source's branding sign has a close ritual counterpart in publicly marked hady.
The hady is held back from reaching its place. Against the source's leader and followed route, this is a concrete animal offering stopped short of its destination.
Among the an'am are animals for bearing burdens and for slaughter. It directly supplies the source's carrying mount and beneficial herd.
People are told to eat and pasture their an'am. The paired human and herd feeding makes the source's merabb and pasture an explicit Qur'anic practice.
Water is driven to barren land so crops feed both cattle and people. The ayah makes pasture a supplied destination for a herd, not merely scenery.
Rain revives a dead land and gives drink to cattle and many people. It ties animal provision to the Lord's life-giving care behind the source's useful herd.
The earth's water, pasture, and mountains are made provision for people and their an'am. It directly places the herd's grazing world within measured provision.
Pasture is brought forth amid the food sequence. This is the source's otlak as a created element of the herd's place.
The preceding vegetation is expressly “provision for you and your cattle”; 80:31 supplies the pasture and this ayah states its shared purpose.
God creates, proportionates, determines, and guides. The source's hâdî is extended from an animal at the front to the Creator's fitting and directing of creatures.
Immediately after divine guidance, God brings forth pasture. The sequence makes guidance and grazing part of one ordering of creaturely life.
God creates pairs and makes ships and an'am for riding. It directly develops the source's binek as a creature made to carry its rider.
Settling on the animals' backs and remembering the One who subjected them gives the source's tame mount an explicit act of riding and acknowledgment of its true owner.
Cattle are made so people ride some and eat some. The source's two functions—carrying and benefit—are stated together.
Livestock contain a lesson: drink comes from within them, they have many benefits, and they are eaten. This unfolds the source's na'am as practical good.
Milk from between waste and blood in cattle is a sign for drinkers, a precise instance of the good and benefit the source assigns to an'am.
Rain produces trees in which people pasture their animals. It supplies the actual grazing act that the source's preferred merabb presumes.
Land creatures and birds are communities, then gathered to their Rabb. The wild herd is not ownerless in the final sense: even animal communities return to their Lord.

Every creature's provision is upon God, who knows its settled place and repository. It answers the source's animal left in a desolate place with the encompassing knowledge and provision of its true owner.
The camel itself is set before the reader as a created sign. It lets the section's concrete camel remain an object of contemplation rather than only a lexical illustration.
The rejecters are likened to startled wild asses. This uses the source's wild-donkey herd sense to picture a human refusal to heed a summons.
Their wild-asses image is completed by flight from a lion. The animal group's panicked dispersal sharpens the source's contrast between being led and running loose.
Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are made leaders who guide by God's command. This is the human counterpart to the source's leading animal whom the rest follow.
Leaders from the Children of Israel guide by God's command while they are steadfast. It specifies what a valid guide at the front of a community is like.
Whoever follows God's guidance will neither go astray nor suffer. The source's flock follows a hâdî; this ayah states the consequence of that following against straying.
God's straight path is to be followed, while other paths scatter people from it. The source's single leader and a camel gone off alone become an explicit route-and-dispersal contrast.
“Worship Me; this is a straight path” joins the source's `na'budu` root to its `ihdinā` route: service to the true owner is the path rather than ownerless wandering.
Jesus says that Allah is his Rabb and theirs, so they should worship Him; this is a straight path. Rabb, service, and route appear in the relation the section develops.
It contrasts one who walks fallen on his face with one who walks upright on a straight path. The bodily route makes the source's guided-versus-stray movement visible.
A man belonging to quarrelling partners is contrasted with one belonging wholly to one man. This turns the source's single herd owner into a sharp image of undivided lordship.

The parable contrasts an owned servant unable to do anything with one freely providing good provision. It makes the source's owner/dependent relation concrete while testing false equivalence with God.
Joseph asks whether scattered masters are better than the One overpowering God. The source's Rabb as owner gains a monotheistic boundary: a herd cannot coherently belong to rival masters.
“Rabb of people” transfers the source's owner-and-nurturer title from the herd image to the human community seeking protection.
“Malik of people,” beside 114:1, repeats the source's two owner titles over one human flock-like community.
God threatens to brand a denier on the snout. The source's recognition brand on a camel becomes its fearful contrary: a public mark of disgrace.
The selected cow is neither subdued to plough nor to irrigate, and has no marking variation. It is a close boundary case for the source's tamed, recognizable working animal.
Garments of tar clothe the criminals. The source's tar-treated, tamed camel is inverted into a human garment of punishment.
The king's missing cup is announced with a camel-load as the reward for returning it. A lost possession, its royal owner, and a camel burden meet in one scene.
The she-camel is sent as a test. It gives the animal a divinely assigned status, unlike the source's camel whose owner is unknown.
Water is divided between the people and the she-camel, with each drinking turn attended. 54:27 names the camel; this ayah gives its concrete share at the herd's water source.
They call their companion, who seizes and hamstrings the she-camel. Harm to the named animal reverses the protected grazing relation in the source.
Thamud hamstrings the she-camel after their command to leave it unharmed. It shows a community refusing the owner-defined limit around the animal.
After hamstringing the she-camel, Thamud receive a final three-day term. The ayah makes violation of the animal's protected status consequential.
The Thamud camel is recalled as a visible sign that they wronged. The source's identifying sign is here a sign-bearing camel whose rejection exposes human blindness.
Salih assigns the she-camel one drinking day and the people another known day. It is a precise pasture-and-water order for a divinely owned animal.
They hamstring the camel and become regretful. The act turns the source's cared-for, useful herd animal into the focus of breached trust.
They deny the messenger and hamstring her; the preceding 91:13 names Allah's she-camel and watering, while this ayah records the violation and its consequence.
Pilgrims name God over the bahīmat al-an'am He has provided and feed the needy. The herd's benefit is explicitly returned to its giver and shared.
Every community has a rite for naming God over livestock He provided. It connects animals as provision with service to the one true God.
Neither the camels' meat nor blood reaches God, but piety does. Against treating the herd as an end in itself, it fixes the owner-directed purpose of 22:36's sacrifice.
An expiation is an equivalent offering from livestock reaching the Ka'bah. The hady word-family ties a concrete animal to an appointed, guided destination.
The sacred offerings and garlands are institutions through which people know God's encompassing knowledge. Marked animal offerings serve a public order rather than private possession.
People assign portions of crops and cattle that God created to God and to alleged partners. It contests human redistribution of a herd whose true source-owner is God.
Invented rules declare certain cattle and crops forbidden and some animals untouchable for riding. This is a direct boundary around who may redefine the herd's use.
God rejects invented named statuses for livestock. The ayah challenges fabricated claims that detach animals from the true owner's command.
Rain produces vegetation eaten by people and cattle, then it becomes as if it had never flourished. The herd's pasture is provisioned but not permanent.
Many creatures do not carry their own provision, yet God provides for them and for people. It gives the source's animal dependence a wider providential frame.
From livestock come portable shelters, furnishings, and wool, fur, and hair. It extends the source's animal benefit beyond transport and food.
God makes paths in the earth “so that you may be guided”; 43:12 then supplies mounts. The adjacent route makes riding animals part of a guided journey.
After riding the subjected animals, people remember their Lord and their return to Him. This gives the source's mount a rider's verbal acknowledgment of its owner.
Beyond riding and eating, livestock carry people to needs held within their hearts. It gives the source's burden-bearing scene an inward as well as geographic destination.
God creates eight mates of livestock and fashions humans in womb stages. The herd is presented as ordered pairs under the same creator who forms hidden human life.
God makes mates for people and for cattle and multiplies them by that order. The verse gives the herd's continuity a created, measured form.
Creatures made from water move by belly, two legs, or four. The source's mount carried on its legs is placed within the Qur'anic differentiation of animal movement.
Wild beasts are gathered. The source's wild, ownerless-looking herds meet an eschatological gathering under a power none of them escapes.
Thamud refuse to follow a single man from among them and call the result error. Their rhetoric reverses the source's herd that needs an acknowledged leader to follow.
Abraham says the One who created him is the One who guides him. The source's animal hâdî opens into the Creator's personal guidance of the creature.
The same speaker says God feeds and gives him drink. Beside 26:78's guidance, this is the owner-provider relation seen in the herd's food and water.
People are commanded to worship their Rabb who created them. The source's `na'budu` and Rabb image is made explicit as a creature's service to its creator-owner.
Jesus calls Allah “my Rabb and your Rabb,” commands worship, and names this a straight path. It tightly joins owner, service, and direction.
Abraham tells his father, “follow me; I will guide you to a straight path.” It is the human form of the source's front-running guide whom others must follow.
The Prophet calls people to a straight path. The ayah supplies a voiced guide in the place where the source imagines an animal leader at the front.
A man comes running from the far end of the city and says, “Follow the messengers.” The movement and summons dramatize a community needing a guide.
He tells them to follow those who ask no payment and are rightly guided. 36:20 provides the summons; this ayah identifies the followers' trustworthy lead.
The believing man in Pharaoh's family says, “Follow me; I will guide you to the way of right conduct.” It is an exact human leader-and-followers counterpart to the source's hâdî.
The Prophet is said to guide to a straight path. This turns the source's request for a leading guide into the messenger's active function.
The jinn hear a scripture that guides to truth and to a straight path. It makes the guide a heard revelation that can lead a responsive group.
The jinn say they heard a wondrous Qur'an that guides to right conduct. The source's requested direction is here received by a community and followed in belief.
Those who hear guidance divide into Muslims who seek right conduct and deviators who become fuel. It states a collective fork between following and going crooked.
God shows the human the way, leaving gratitude or denial open. The source's guided herd image becomes a morally answerable human route.
The human is shown the two paths. It gives a compact counterpart to the source's one leading route and the possibility of going loose from it.
“Upon Us is guidance” identifies the true source of the direction for which the section asks.
The addressee is found in need of direction and then guided. It is the personal movement out of the source's dalālah scene.
Those who follow God's guidance have no fear or grief. The source's lead animal becomes a covenantal pattern: safety belongs to following divine direction.
It names one who has “strayed from the evenness of the way.” This is a precise route-form of the source's escaped camel and its dallīn.
Talut is appointed malik over a reluctant people. The source's M-L-K word-family as a front leader gains a human political instance.
A sign confirms Talut's kingship. Beside 2:247's malik, public recognition of the leader echoes the source's identifying mark on a herd animal.
Talut sets out with his troops and tests their drinking at a river. The king of 2:247 is shown actually leading a group through a water boundary.
Needy people are recognized by their sīmā. The source's recognition brand is transferred to a human sign by which a hidden condition becomes legible.
God is Mālik al-mulk, giving and taking authority. It distinguishes the source's creaturely mālik from the one who owns sovereignty itself.
Those who obey God and the messenger are with those God has blessed. It gives the source's an'amta a company formed by obedience to divine leadership.
Moses tells his people to remember God's favor when He made prophets among them and made them kings. Ni'mah and M-L-K appear together as bestowed, not self-owned, standing.
Abraham says that without his Lord's guidance he would be among the erring people. It directly makes Rabb the rescue from the source's dalālah.
After listing earlier prophets, the Prophet is told to follow their guidance. The source's following herd gains a concrete chain of exemplary guides.
Two of camels and two of cattle are named while false prohibitions are challenged. It keeps the source's camel within a dispute over who may claim authority over livestock.
Satan vows to sit on God's straight path to obstruct people. The source's route is shown as a place where a rival leader tries to turn a following group away.
People on the Heights recognize groups by their marks. Like the source's branded camel, an outward sign identifies a person in a decisive gathering.
The people on the Heights recognize arrogant people by their marks; 7:46 establishes the sign-based recognition, and this ayah applies it to a named group.
The man who follows desire is likened to a panting dog whether driven off or left alone. An animal image exposes a human who refuses elevation through the signs.
If idols are called to guidance, they do not follow. The source's leader-and-herd relation is reversed in a summons that produces no following.
The malik's dream stages seven fat cows consumed by seven lean ones. Kingly rule and a cattle scene meet, extending the source's M-L-K and herd vocabulary.
Joseph's brothers find their goods restored and ask for an additional camel-load. The camel appears as a measured carrying unit within an owned provision economy.
After the livestock benefits of 16:5–16, people cannot count God's ni'mah. The source's lexical move from an'am to benefit receives its immediate Qur'anic horizon.
Every community receives a messenger commanding worship of God and avoidance of false gods; some are guided and some deserve error. It is herd-scale leadership with a real split in response.
Every people will be called with its imam. The source's front animal becomes a final-account image of communities identified with the guide they followed.
Whomever God guides is guided, and no guiding protector is found for one He lets stray. It gives the source's lost creature an absolute limit on substitute leadership.
Moses says his Rabb neither goes astray nor forgets. The source's lost/unknown camel is countered by a Lord whose knowledge never loses its object.
Whoever takes Satan as ally is led astray and guided toward the Blaze. It is the anti-hādī: a leader whose following has the opposite destination.
The arrogant person turns aside to lead people from God's way. The bodily turn makes a crooked front-runner the contrary of the source's guiding leader.
God's hand holds the dominion of every thing, while He protects and cannot be protected against. This cosmic ownership supplies the force behind calling every thing's Rabb its mālik.
Moses sets out toward Madyan asking his Lord for a sound way; the next scene, 28:23, brings him to the watering flocks. The traveler's request leads into a pastoral encounter.

The parable asks whether people would accept those their right hands possess as equal partners in provision. It uses ownership dependency to reject divided lordship, like the source's single herd owner.
The condemned say they obeyed masters and great ones, who led them astray from the path. It is a direct false-leader version of the herd's following.
The dominion of every thing is in God's hand and all return to Him. It completes 36:71's human ownership of cattle with God's prior ownership of all things.
The wrongdoers are gathered with those like them and what they worshipped. Its gathering language begins a contrary herd movement toward judgment.
The angels are told to guide them to the path of Hell. Following 37:22's gathering, this is a terrible inversion of the source's sought-after guide.
David recognizes that asking to add one ewe to ninety-nine is wrongdoing. The 38:23 flock dispute becomes a moral limit on a stronger owner's claim.
David is made a successor and warned not to follow desire, lest it lead him astray from God's way. A human leader must himself remain guided.
Thamud are given guidance but prefer blindness to it. Their choice places the source's camel-owning community on the side of refusing direction.
Disbelievers eat and enjoy as cattle eat, while the Fire is their lodging. The source's animal benefit becomes a warning against human life reduced to unguided consumption.
Those who are guided receive increased guidance and their piety. The ayah depicts guidance as a path that can deepen for those who stay with it.
Some turn back after guidance has become clear, following Satan's inducement. This is a human version of departing from a recognized guide.
Hypocrites could be known by their marks and by the tone of speech. The source's identifying wasm becomes a moral sign that exposes a hidden affiliation.
The believers have a sīmā on their faces from prostration. It gives the source's recognition-mark a devotional rather than proprietary form.
The Prophet is declared neither astray nor misled. A true guide is first distinguished from the source's dallīn.
People follow only conjecture and desire though guidance has come from their Lord. It names a rival following that leaves the received route.
Criminals are recognized by their marks before being seized. The source's visible identifier is recast as recognition in judgment.
Those charged with Torah but not carrying it are compared to a donkey carrying books. The burden-bearing animal exposes a human failure to be led by what it carries.
The earth is made compliant, people walk its paths and eat its provision. The source's tamed animal is broadened to a tamed terrain that carries its walkers along routes.
Had people remained on the straight way, they would have been given abundant water. The route is linked to provision in a way that recalls pasture and watering.
The sparks are likened to yellow camels. The concrete camel's color and mass are turned into an image of the Fire, not a herd under care.
The pasture of 87:4 is then made dark debris. Its change limits any reading of the grazing ground as self-sustaining or permanent.
The command to speak of the Lord's ni'mah makes the source's benefit vocabulary an act of acknowledgment rather than mere possession.
A camel cannot pass through the eye of a needle before the arrogant enter the Garden. The source's familiar animal becomes a physical image of an impossible boundary.
Trained hunting animals are taught what to catch for their keeper. Their learned obedience gives a concrete counterpart to the source's tamed animal that follows a leader and serves an owner.

It asks whether the One who guides to truth is more worthy of being followed than one who cannot guide unless guided. This gives the source's hâdî and following herd an explicit criterion for a true leader.

God makes paths through the earth, sends down water, and brings out paired plants; 20:54 then tells people to pasture their livestock. This ayah supplies the route and growth that make the next ayah's grazing possible.
After 24:45 differentiates animal movement, this ayah says God guides whom He wills to a straight path. It joins creaturely motion to the section's requested direction without conflating the two.
God brings out the earth's water and pasture; 79:33 identifies that created order as provision for people and their cattle. This ayah contributes the grazing ground itself.
God creates and proportionates; 87:3 then says He determines and guides. The ayah contributes the making-fit side of the source's guide-and-creature image.
Those who follow the messenger, support him, and follow the light sent down with him are called successful. It gives the source's following relation a revealed guide and a communal response.
People are commanded to believe in the messenger and follow him so that they may be guided. It directly joins following a leader to receiving guidance.
Among the created are a community that guides by truth and acts justly by it. This supplies a collective form of reliable guidance rather than a lone animal leader.
Following 12:39's rival masters, Joseph says judgment belongs only to God and that people are commanded to worship Him alone. It gives the source's owner-and-service relation its exclusive object.
The Prophet calls to God with insight, “I and whoever follows me.” The ayah makes a guided way a visible chain of leader and followers.
After calling the Prophet a warner, it says that every people has a guide. The source's hâdî is thereby widened from a herd's front animal to a people-specific guide.
All moving creatures in the heavens and earth prostrate to God. The source's `na'budu` and tamed-animal relation meet in creatures whose submission belongs to their maker.
Moses and Aaron are told to announce peace for whoever follows guidance. It attaches a concrete promised outcome to the source's act of following the guide.
In the sacrificial-rites passage, benefits remain in the offerings until an appointed term, then their destination is the Ancient House. It adds duration and destination to the animal scene of 22:36.
Birds in flight each know their own prayer and glorification. An animal collective has an ordered response to its Lord, extending the source's herd-under-owner image without making birds livestock.
An ant warns its community to enter their dwellings before Solomon's forces arrive. Like the source's bee and herd details, it stages an animal community receiving a protective lead from within.
God creates and disperses living creatures through the heavens and earth, and can gather them when He wills. The wild herd's apparent freedom is set inside a larger divine power to gather.
Pharaoh makes his people compliant and they obey him. It is a false human herd-leader: obedience follows a deceiving ruler rather than a trustworthy guide.

The simile describes a recipient hearing only a call and cry. Its animal referent is implicit rather than named, so it only tentatively parallels a herd that must recognize its caller rather than hear meaningless noise.
The ayah notices varied colors among beasts and livestock. It offers an indirect natural counterpart to the source's visible identifying mark, though color here is not an ownership brand.
